questions.stem: « Avez-vous une chambre libre pour ce soir ? » What is the traveller asking?
options: whether the room has been cleaned
when the room must be vacated
whether a room is free tonight
how much a room costs tonight
questions.explanation: « Une chambre libre » is a vacant room, and « pour ce soir » means for tonight. Checking out is « libérer la chambre ».

questions.stem: At a campsite: « Je voudrais réserver un emplacement pour une tente. » What is being booked?
options: a pitch for a tent
a tent to borrow
a cabin with four beds
a parking space
questions.explanation: « Un emplacement » is a numbered site or pitch at a campsite. Renting a cabin would be « louer un bungalow ».

questions.stem: « Qu'est-ce que vous me conseillez de visiter ? » What is the speaker asking?
options: for a map of the city centre
for the price of a guided tour
for directions to the station
for advice on what to visit
questions.explanation: « Conseiller » means to advise or recommend. It is a useful question at « l'office de tourisme ».

questions.stem: « Si vous passez par là, ce village vaut le détour ! » What does the speaker mean?
options: The road to the village is closed
The village is best avoided
The village is well worth a visit
The village is hard to find
questions.explanation: « Valoir le détour » means it is worth going out of your way for. Guidebooks use it as a recommendation.

questions.stem: What is « une visite guidée »?
options: a guided tour
a guidebook
a tour guide's fee
a self-guided walk
questions.explanation: « Une visite guidée » is a tour with a guide. A guidebook is « un guide », the same word as the person.

questions.stem: « La vue est à couper le souffle, mais en août, c'est envahi de touristes. » How does the writer evaluate the place?
options: a breathtaking view, and peaceful all through August
a view spoilt by the tourists who live there
a breathtaking view, but overrun with tourists in August
a disappointing view, and empty of tourists in August
questions.explanation: « À couper le souffle » means breathtaking, and « envahi de » means overrun with. « Mais » sets the drawback against the praise.

questions.stem: « Ce voyage m'a appris à être plus autonome et à sortir de ma zone de confort. » What benefit of travel is described?
options: finding that home is better than anywhere else
becoming more independent and trying new things
learning to plan trips that are always comfortable
making the most of five-star hotels abroad
questions.explanation: « Autonome » means independent, and « sortir de sa zone de confort » is to step outside what feels familiar and safe.

questions.stem: Which Paris museum displays the Mona Lisa, « La Joconde »?
options: le Louvre
le musée d'Orsay
le Centre Pompidou
le musée Rodin
questions.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci's « La Joconde » hangs in the Louvre, a former royal palace. The musée d'Orsay is known for Impressionist paintings.

questions.stem: What is Mont-Saint-Michel?
options: a château in the Loire Valley
a Roman arena in the south of France
an abbey on a tidal island off Normandy
a ski resort high in the French Alps
questions.explanation: Mont-Saint-Michel is a rocky island crowned by a medieval abbey, in a bay between Normandy and Brittany. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of France's most visited places.

questions.stem: Why must visitors to Mont-Saint-Michel's bay take care with tide times?
options: The abbey opens only for one hour at low tide
The tide changes only once a year, in winter
The tides are among Europe's strongest and come in fast
The bay is closed to visitors when the tide is out
questions.explanation: The bay has some of the largest tidal ranges in Europe, and the sea can sweep across the sands quickly. Walkers crossing the bay are advised to go with a guide.

questions.stem: Vieux-Québec, the historic heart of Québec City, is a UNESCO World Heritage site. What is it known for?
options: its fortified walls and old stone streets
its glass skyscrapers and business towers
its tropical beaches and coral reefs
its volcano and black sand beaches
questions.explanation: Old Québec has the only city walls still standing in North America north of Mexico, and narrow streets of stone houses dating from the French colonial era.

questions.stem: In Québec City, what is the Château Frontenac?
options: a grand hotel overlooking the St Lawrence River
a castle built by the kings of France in the 1600s
the building where Québec's parliament sits
a ski lodge in the mountains north of the city
questions.explanation: Despite its name, the Château Frontenac is a hotel, opened in the 1890s by a railway company. Named after a governor of New France, it is the city's best-known landmark.

questions.stem: What is expected when you walk into a small shop in France?
options: to say « Bonjour » to the shopkeeper
to say nothing until you pay
to shake hands with every staff member
to leave your bag at the door
questions.explanation: Greeting the shopkeeper with « Bonjour » (and « Au revoir » on leaving) is basic politeness in France. Ignoring them can seem rude.

questions.stem: You meet your penfriend's father for the first time. How should you address him?
options: with vous and his first name
with vous: « Bonjour, monsieur »
with tu and his first name, like a friend
with tu: « Salut, ça va ? »
questions.explanation: Adults you do not know are addressed with vous and « monsieur » or « madame » until they invite you to use tu.

questions.stem: At a French family meal, where is bread usually placed?
options: on the tablecloth beside your plate
on a small side plate at your left
in your lap until the cheese course
in a basket kept in the kitchen
questions.explanation: French tables rarely have side plates: bread sits directly on the table beside your plate, and is used to push food and wipe up sauce.

questions.stem: During a meal in France, where should your hands be?
options: on your chair while you wait for the meal
on the table, with wrists resting on the edge
in your lap, out of sight, between courses
behind your back while others are eating
questions.explanation: French etiquette keeps both hands visible, wrists on the edge of the table. Hands in your lap, the habit in some English-speaking countries, can look odd.

questions.stem: When do people say « Bon appétit ! »?
options: when someone sneezes
at the start of a meal
at the end of a meal
when the bill arrives
questions.explanation: « Bon appétit » is said as everyone starts eating. When someone sneezes, people say « À tes souhaits ! » or « À vos souhaits ! ».

questions.stem: You are invited to dinner at a French home at 8 pm. When is it polite to arrive?
options: an hour late, after the starter
a little after eight, but not before
half an hour early, to help with the cooking
exactly on the stroke of eight
questions.explanation: Arriving a few minutes late, « le quart d'heure de politesse », gives hosts time to finish preparing. Arriving early can catch them unready.

questions.stem: On a French restaurant menu, « service compris » means what?
options: The restaurant offers table service only
Customers must serve themselves
The service charge is already in the prices
Waiters must be tipped at least twenty per cent
questions.explanation: In France, menu prices include service by law, so a tip is a small optional extra for good service rather than an expected percentage.

questions.stem: Who is « Bonhomme Carnaval »?
options: the carnival king who leads the parade in Nice
a puppet character in Lyon's theatre
the clown who leads the Paris circus
the snowman mascot of the Québec Winter Carnival
questions.explanation: Bonhomme, a smiling snowman in a red cap and sash, presides over the Carnaval de Québec, one of the world's largest winter festivals.

questions.stem: During Lyon's Fête des Lumières, around 8 December, what do many residents traditionally place on their windowsills?
options: pots of red geraniums
French flags and bunting
small candles in coloured glasses
carved pumpkins with lanterns
questions.explanation: Lyon families set « lumignons », candles in small glass holders, on their windows. The festival now also draws crowds with large light installations across the city.

questions.stem: What happens during the « bataille de fleurs » at the Nice Carnival?
options: Florists sell flowers at half price
People on decorated floats throw flowers to the crowd
Teams of gardeners compete to grow the largest flowers
Spectators throw rotten fruit at the floats
questions.explanation: In February, flower-covered floats parade along the seafront, and their riders throw thousands of fresh flowers to spectators.

questions.stem: On the evening of 14 July, what do French towns traditionally hold?
options: fireworks and public dances
parades of carnival giants
candlelit church processions
pumpkin carving contests
questions.explanation: The national day ends with « le feu d'artifice » (fireworks) and « les bals », including the famous firefighters' balls, « les bals des pompiers ».

questions.stem: In French tradition, who is said to bring chocolate eggs at Easter?
options: the tooth fairy, for good children
the church bells, returning from Rome
Father Christmas, on a second visit in spring
the Easter bunny, and no one else
questions.explanation: The story says church bells fall silent and fly to Rome before Easter, then return on Easter morning dropping eggs in gardens. Some regions, such as Alsace, also have an Easter hare.

questions.stem: What is a « poisson d'avril »?
options: an April Fools' joke, such as a paper fish stuck on someone's back
a traditional fish dish eaten at Easter in the coastal towns
a fishing competition held on the first of April
a spring festival for the opening of the fishing season
questions.explanation: On 1 April, children try to stick paper fish on people's backs, and the media publish hoax stories, all called « poissons d'avril ».

questions.stem: On 1 November, la Toussaint, what do many French families do?
options: dress up in costumes and go trick-or-treating
light bonfires to welcome the winter
exchange gifts with close friends
place chrysanthemums on family graves
questions.explanation: La Toussaint (All Saints' Day) is a public holiday when families visit cemeteries to honour their dead, which is why chrysanthemums are linked with mourning in France.

questions.stem: « Chaque année, tout le quartier prépare la fête : c'est ce qui nous rassemble. » What does the festival do for the neighbourhood?
options: It divides the neighbours
It raises money for repairs
It attracts foreign tourists
It brings people together
questions.explanation: « Rassembler » means to bring together, and « c'est ce qui » emphasises it. Preparing the festival gives the community a sense of belonging.

questions.stem: In France, where must the legal wedding ceremony take place?
options: anywhere the couple chooses, even a beach
in a law court, in front of a judge
at the town hall, before any religious ceremony
in a church, before the couple go to the town hall
questions.explanation: Only a civil wedding at « la mairie », led by the mayor or a deputy, is legally valid, and it must come before any religious ceremony, reflecting the separation of church and state.

questions.stem: What are « les dragées » given at French baptisms and weddings?
options: printed menus
sugar-coated almonds
small bunches of flowers
silver coins
questions.explanation: Guests receive « dragées », almonds in a hard sugar coating, often in small bags or boxes as a keepsake of the celebration.

questions.stem: In France, what does reaching « la majorité » at 18 mean?
options: having to leave the family home
starting the final year of lycée
becoming a legal adult, with the right to vote
being allowed to start learning to drive a car
questions.explanation: At 18, young people become legal adults: they can vote and sign contracts alone. Learning to drive can start well before 18.

questions.stem: « Pour beaucoup de jeunes, obtenir le permis de conduire est un vrai rite de passage : c'est le début de la liberté. » What is the writer's point?
options: Young people no longer care about driving
Driving lessons are a burden for most families
The licence test is a religious ceremony
A driving licence marks a step towards independence
questions.explanation: « Un rite de passage » marks a move to a new stage of life. Getting a licence is presented as the start of freedom.

questions.stem: What is the Alliance française?
options: a military alliance between France and several of its former colonies
a French bank with branches in many countries
a political party that wants France to leave the EU
a network that teaches French and promotes French culture worldwide
questions.explanation: Founded in Paris in 1883, the Alliance française runs language schools and cultural centres around the world, including in Australian cities.

questions.stem: On which date is the Journée internationale de la Francophonie celebrated?
options: 1 May
21 June
20 March
14 July
questions.explanation: The International Day of La Francophonie, on 20 March, celebrates the French language and the communities that share it. 14 July is France's national day and 21 June the Fête de la musique.

questions.stem: Which Frenchman revived the modern Olympic Games, founding the International Olympic Committee in 1894?
options: Jules Rimet
Louis Braille
Gustave Eiffel
Pierre de Coubertin
questions.explanation: Pierre de Coubertin founded the IOC in Paris in 1894, and the first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896. Jules Rimet launched football's World Cup.

questions.stem: Which system of measurement, now used in almost every country, was introduced in France after the Revolution?
options: the metric system
the imperial system
the 24-hour clock
the Gregorian calendar
questions.explanation: Revolutionary France created the metre and the kilogram to replace a confusing mix of local units. The Gregorian calendar dates from 1582, long before.

questions.stem: English uses « déjà vu », « rendezvous » and « ballet ». What does this show?
options: English has replaced these French words
These words were invented in England
French borrowed these words from English
French has enriched the English language
questions.explanation: English has taken thousands of words from French, especially in food, fashion, the arts and law. It is one sign of French influence in the world.

questions.stem: « Au Québec comme en Louisiane, des associations se battent pour que le français reste vivant. » What is being described?
options: fights breaking out between French speakers
a campaign to replace English with French in France
the decline of English in Louisiana
efforts to keep French alive in North America
questions.explanation: « Se battre pour que » here means to campaign so that, followed by the subjunctive « reste ». Associations keep French culture alive where English dominates.
